terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Build both .cpp files into one program here and run it, after each move.

tasks.title: Move the repair's struct into repair.h
tasks.description:
Move the struct `Repair` out of `src/main.cpp` into `src/repair.h`, under `// Task 1`, with every member as it was. Put it inside an include guard: its `#ifndef` and `#define` at the top of the file, and its `#endif` on the last line. `repair.h` also includes what it needs for `std::string`. `main.cpp` keeps its `#include "repair.h"`.

Check writes a program of its own that includes `repair.h` twice, before anything else, makes repairs from it and reads their members. It also looks at whether `main.cpp` still writes `Repair` itself.
nextSteps: Cut the struct out of `main.cpp` and paste it under `// Task 1` in `repair.h`.
Add the `#include` that `std::string` comes from, above the struct.
Write the guard's two lines at the very top of `repair.h`, and `#endif` at its very end.
Build both files with the terminal's command and run the program.
hints: A header is read by every file that includes it, wherever that file includes it, so it includes what it uses itself: here `<string>`.
A guard is three lines: `#ifndef REPAIR_H` and `#define REPAIR_H` at the top, `#endif` at the bottom. The name after `#define` is the same as the one after `#ifndef`.
The file is `#ifndef REPAIR_H`, `#define REPAIR_H`, the comments, `#include <string>`, the struct as it was in `main.cpp`, the other tasks, and `#endif` on the last line.

tasks.title: Move minutesText into repair.h and repair.cpp
tasks.description:
Move `minutesText` out of `src/main.cpp`. Its declaration goes in `src/repair.h` under `// Task 2`, and its whole body in `src/repair.cpp` under `// Task 2`, unchanged. At the top of `repair.cpp`, above its first `// Task` comment, include `repair.h`.

Check builds its own program, which includes `repair.h`, together with your `repair.cpp`, calls `minutesText` with minutes of its own and reads what it gives back. It also looks at whether `main.cpp` still writes `minutesText` itself. Check puts a `Repair` of its own where Task 1's is, so this task is judged on its own.
nextSteps: Cut `minutesText` out of `main.cpp` and paste it under `// Task 2` in `repair.cpp`.
Include `repair.h` at the top of `repair.cpp`, with double quotes.
In `repair.h`, under `// Task 2`, write the function's first line with a semicolon.
Build both `.cpp` files and run the program.
hints: A declaration is the first line of a function with a semicolon in place of its body. It tells every file that includes it that the function exists, and what it takes and gives back.
A header of your own is included with double quotes, `#include "repair.h"`: angle brackets look only among the compiler's own headers.
`repair.h` gets `std::string minutesText(int minutes);` and `repair.cpp` gets `#include "repair.h"` at its top and the whole function under `// Task 2`.

tasks.title: Declare and write minutesOver
tasks.description:
Add a new function, `minutesOver`, in two places. In `src/repair.h` under `// Task 3`, declare it: it takes a repair as a reference to a `const Repair` and the minutes Dorrit quoted as an `int`, and gives back an `int`. In `src/repair.cpp` under `// Task 3`, write it: it gives back how many minutes the repair has gone over the quote, or `0` when it is within it. With 75 minutes on the repair and a quote of 60, it gives back 15.

Check builds its own program, which includes `repair.h`, together with your `repair.cpp`, calls `minutesOver` with repairs and quotes of its own, and reads what it gives back.
nextSteps: Write the declaration in `repair.h`: the first line, with a semicolon.
Write the whole function in `repair.cpp`, with the same first line.
Give back 0 when the minutes are within the quote, and the difference when they are over.
Call it from `main` and build both files.
hints: The declaration and the definition say the same thing: the same name, the same parameter types and the same type back. When they differ, the linker finds no function to match the declaration.
Ask first whether the minutes are within the quote, and give back 0 then. Otherwise the minutes minus the quote is how far over it went.
`repair.h` gets `int minutesOver(const Repair& repair, int quoted);` and `repair.cpp` the same line with a body: `if (repair.minutes <= quoted) { return 0; } return repair.minutes - quoted;`.
